title: Wasserstein residuals: Learning Gradient Flows from Population Dynamics
claim: Prior chord-based predictors cut straight across curved dynamics; our method follows the true curved trajectory through sparse snapshots.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared axes, ground truth then ours then baseline
description: A shared legend sits on top: gray dots for data snapshots, a green line for the Stitching KDE-particle trajectory, and a dark red line for the Lightspeed JKO OT-chord. Below are three side-by-side 2D contour plots over x1 (-4 to 6) and x2 (-2 to 2), each showing a potential landscape in a warm-to-cool colormap. Panel (a), the true potential V*, has a sinusoidal valley with five snapshot clusters colored from purple to yellow-green along it. Panel (b), Stitching V^θ, overlays smooth green curves that follow the valley between the clusters. Panel (c), Lightspeed V^θ, overlays straight red chords that cut across the valley. The contrast between curved green paths and straight red lines draws the eye first.
caption: Stitching recovers curvature that JKO chord predictors miss. Sparse SDE snapshots (N = 20) on a sinusoidal valley at t ∈{0, 5, 10, 20, 30}. (a) True potential. (b) Stitching’s trajectory tracks the valley. (c) Lightspeed (Terpin et al., 2024) does not capture the curved trajectories of the particles; see Section 5.1.
abstract: Reconstructing population dynamics is a central problem in the physical and data sciences. Often, the dynamics are modeled as a Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF): a curve of distributions driven by an energy functional. Though there are multiple mathematical characterizations of a WGF, the dominant algorithmic approach relies on the Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) scheme. JKO-based methods are inflexible to time discretisation and require solving costly optimal transport problems. We take a residual approach, enforcing the continuity equations via a non-negative loss function whose minimum is the WGF. Combined with a data-fitting divergence, this gives a single global objective. This perspective unifies several existing methods and leads to a new particle-based method, stitching, that is simulation-free and robust to large gaps between observations. We demonstrate that the stitching method achieves state-of-the-art performance across trajectory inference benchmarks. For code see github.com/BasisResearch/wasserstein-residuals.
